title: Anti-Zeno boost in an autonomous quantized-piston thermal machine
abstract: Anti-Zeno enhancement of quantum heat machines has been established for working fluids driven by an external classical field, but whether the same quantum advantage survives when a quantized piston replaces the classical drive has remained open. Here we study an autonomous thermal machine in which a two-level working fluid is coupled to a quantized harmonic piston and to two spectrally separated reservoirs, without external modulation. We derive a finite-time master equation for the resulting carrier and sideband channels, whose rates interpolate between the Zeno, anti-Zeno, and Markovian regimes as the coupling time is varied. For an initially coherent piston, the machine charges the piston and generates more ergotropy than the Markovian reference in the anti-Zeno window. Reversing the same retained channels turns the device into a finite-resource refrigerator with enhanced cooling. The anti-Zeno effect therefore increases the rate of operation while leaving the underlying carrier and sideband energy ratios unchanged. These channel ratios remain consistent with the usual Carnot bounds over the operating regimes considered here. Our results establish finite-time reservoir sampling as a mechanism for enhancing autonomous thermal-machine operation with a quantized piston, without external modulation.
summary: This paper analyzes an autonomous thermal machine driven by a quantized piston instead of an external field. By utilizing the anti-Zeno effect within a finite-time framework, the authors demonstrate that the engine's ability to generate useful work (ergotropy) is enhanced beyond classical predictions. This establishes finite-time reservoir sampling as a novel mechanism for improving quantum heat engine and refrigerator performance.
main_problem: The study investigates whether the quantum advantage provided by the anti-Zeno effect persists when a classical drive in a thermal machine is replaced by a quantized piston, enabling autonomous operation.
main_result: Finite-time reservoir sampling enhances ergotropy generation in the engine mode beyond Markovian limits, and this mechanism can be reversed to achieve enhanced quantum refrigeration without external modulation.
method: The authors derive and analyze a finite-time master equation for the system dynamics, comparing results across Zeno, anti-Zeno, and Markovian regimes.
model_or_system: The model is an autonomous thermal machine comprising a two-level working fluid coupled to a quantized harmonic piston and interacting with two spectrally separated thermal reservoirs (hot and cold).
key_observables: Ergotropy (useful work content), energy balance equations ($\dot{E}_{	ext{TLS}} + \dot{E}_P = \dot{Q}_h + \dot{Q}_c$), and channel-energy ratios.
important_parameters: Coupling time ($	au_c$), reservoir temperatures ($T_h, T_c$), and the characteristic timescales defining the operational regimes ($\Delta_{sb}^{-1} \ll 	au_c \lesssim 	au_B$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed without external modulation of the system parameters.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the setup, showing the TLS coupled to the piston and reservoirs, and depicts the anti-Zeno mechanism enhancing rates compared to Markovian sampling.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (Hamiltonians), derives the finite-time master equation using TCL2 methods, analyzes energy conservation for both engine and refrigerator cycles, and compares the resulting performance metrics (ergotropy) against long-time Markovian limits.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics by extending known effects (like Zeno/Anti-Zeno) into complex mechanical systems, providing a mechanism for enhancing energy conversion efficiency in fundamental quantum engines.
